one_liner: Rust parser-combinator library; its own benchmarks show parity at best with handwritten C HTTP parsers, not a win.
what_it_does: nom builds parsers by composing small functions (tag, take_while, alt, many0, length_value, be_u32 and so on) over &[u8], &str or bit streams; each parser returns the remaining input plus a value, with Incomplete reported in the streaming variants so the same grammar can run on partial network data. Outputs borrow from the input, errors are pluggable (nom-language adds VerboseError and precedence parsing), and the crate builds for no_std. It is not a drop-in for any C parser: you write the grammar in Rust, and nom 8 replaced closure-style calls with a Parser trait (`combinator(arg).parse(input)`).
how_it_is_fast: Combinators are generic and marked #[inline(always)], so LLVM monomorphises a grammar into straight-line code with no runtime parser objects; outputs are zero-copy subslices, and byte or substring searches go through memchr. nom 8 adds an OutputMode with a Check mode that runs a parser without building its output or error value (used where combinators discard results), which the docs say greatly reduces generated code and memory. nom itself has no SIMD scanning: the 'nom (optimized)' HTTP experiment that edged out picohttpparser used hand-written unrolled loops and an SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI scanner defined in the benchmark repo, not in nom.
when_to_use: Binary formats and protocols in Rust (TLV, X.509, pcap, TLS records, MP4 box headers) where memory safety and correct handling of partial input matter more than the last 10-50% of throughput.
Porting a handwritten C parser into a Rust codebase when parity-class speed is acceptable: idiomatic nom 4 ran 1.06-1.47x slower than Joyent http-parser while building heap-allocated header vectors.
Streaming parsers fed chunk by chunk (the streaming modules return Incomplete instead of a wrong result at buffer end).
no_std or embedded targets: default-features = false, with alloc optional for the Vec-building combinators.
Prototyping configuration or language parsers that need good error positions (nom-language VerboseError, nom_locate).
when_not_to_use: When the goal is beating C: in the same table idiomatic nom was 4.4-5.2x slower than picohttpparser (889 vs 170 ns one_test, 59,918 vs 13,260 ns small_test, derived from page data), and the only nom result faster than picohttpparser is the SIMD experiment discussed under gotchas.
JSON: serde_json 1.0.32 beat the nom 5 JSON parser on every &str input in parser_benchmarks/json (canada.json 12.4 vs 27.7 ms); use a dedicated JSON library.
Float-heavy grammars on nom 7.1+: the changelog says moving back to the standard library float parser was a performance regression and recommends recognize_float plus another converter.

Teams that need fast upstream fixes: last commit 2025-08-26, about 50 open pull requests, and issue #1822 (possible nom 8 slowdown versus nom 7, maintainer suspects missing #[inline]) has been open since February 2025.
Grammars written in idiomatic many0/many1 style that collect Vec values per item: every request in the HTTP benchmark allocated a Vec of headers plus a Vec per header value.

integration.form: crate (nom on crates.io; nom-language companion crate)
integration.dependencies: memchr 2.3 (default features off; nom's std feature enables memchr/std)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.65 for nom 8 (edition 2021); MSRV changes only with a major release
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no_std with default-features = false, alloc feature for allocating combinators
integration.thread_safety: not documented; parsers are functions or small structs over borrowed input, with no shared global state in the code read

gotchas: The record's caveat that 'the C harness mallocs and memcpys every header' is wrong: in parser_benchmarks/http/joyent_http_parser/main.c the LOOK_BUSY define is commented out and the Makefile (gcc -Ofast -O3 -DNDEBUG) does not set it, so the http-parser callbacks only count messages. Idiomatic nom-http, by contrast, builds a Vec<Header> per request and a Vec<&[u8]> per header value inside the timed loop. The C side did less work and still won by 1.06-1.47x.

The HTTP table mixes statistics and inputs: the C driver prints the arithmetic mean of 1,000 timed calls with no warm-up and a 'variance' loop that assigns instead of accumulating (acc2 = ... rather than +=), so the C '+/-' values reflect one sample; the Rust rows are bencher medians with a max-min range; and the Rust one_test literals use bare LF line endings (8 bytes shorter) while the C one_test uses CRLF. In the same table the httparse driver calls req.parse(buf) on the whole buffer instead of the advanced slice, so its small_test and bigger_test rows re-parse the first request.

nom-optimized is benchmark-repo code, not nom: its take_while1_unrolled and take_while1_simd helpers use get_unchecked and read one byte past the slice end when the whole remaining input matches and its length is a multiple of 8 (or 16), or is empty; take_while1_simd loads 16 bytes from a 4- or 6-byte ranges constant; the SIMD URL scan accepts bytes 0x80-0xFF that the scalar is_url_token fallback rejects. Every token in the measured inputs ends before a line terminator, so the overreads were not triggered in the timed runs, but the code needs nightly feature gates (const_fn, stdsimd, cfg_target_feature) and nom 4 macros removed in nom 7, so it does not build today. Its picohttpparser opponent (pico-sys 0.0.1, gcc::compile_library with no -msse4.2) had its __SSE4_2__ paths compiled out.

The MP4 '135x over hammer' row compares nom 0.1.6 (2015), which slices top-level box bodies without reading them, against a hammer grammar that turns every body byte into an h_uint8 token, uses the size field (which includes the 8-byte header) as the body length and re-parses ftyp inside an action; the checked-in nom-mp4 code is now nom 5 with jemalloc, so the table cannot be reproduced.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the systems-and-safety siblings is a parser toolkit; pick nom when you need a general grammar for a binary or text format in safe Rust. If the workload is JSON, the serde sibling (kostya/benchmarks json) is the tested fast path, and for raw HTTP/1.x header parsing a dedicated parser such as picohttpparser beat idiomatic nom by 4.4-5.2x in nom's own table.
verified_claims_summary: nom's README claims parity with handwritten C ('just as fast') with no numbers; the linked parser_benchmarks tables (late-2013 MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz quad-core Core i7, compiler versions not stated) show idiomatic nom 4 1.06-1.47x slower than Joyent http-parser built with gcc -Ofast -O3 on four HTTP request inputs. The nom-optimized experiment's 1.06-1.14x edge over picohttpparser is within the error bars, uses custom SSE4.2 code against a picohttpparser build without its SSE4.2 path, and the 2015 MP4 comparison against the C combinator library hammer measures different work, so no measurement shows nom beating C.
status_note: Stale but massively used (about 786 million crates.io downloads, 8.0.0 released 2025-01-26, last commit 2025-08-26, about 50 open pull requests); MIT-licensed and safe to depend on for correctness-first parsing, but its speed-versus-C claim rests on 2015-2019 benchmarks that show parity or a loss.
